scenes.tts: A water flea is transparent. Put an infected one under a microscope, and you can watch its blood cells swallow invading yeast spores. Where the cells destroyed the spores, the infection stopped. Where spores grew into budding yeast, the flea died.
scenes.visual: Transparent flea outline; blood cells and needle-shaped spores appear; cells engulf spores; flea shrinks left (spores destroyed, infection stops) beside a second flea filled with budding yeast (flea dies).

scenes.tts: Innate defenses are ready before an organism meets a particular microbe. In mammalian airways, mucus traps microbes, and cilia carry it out. A microbe that gets through meets a phagocyte, a cell that engulfs particles. The microbe sits in a bubble, the phagosome. Lysosomes, sacs of digestive enzymes, fuse with it and kill the microbe.
scenes.visual: Airway lining bar with mucus and cilia trapping microbes; one gets through, a phagocyte engulfs it into a phagosome, lysosomes fuse, microbe disappears.

scenes.tts: In mammals, complement is a set of proteins in blood plasma. When C three is cut, its large piece, C three b, sticks to a microbe and marks it for eating. The small pieces, C three a and C five a, drift away and promote inflammation. Later pieces can punch holes in susceptible microbes. Interferons from virus-infected cells put nearby cells into an antiviral state. Natural killer cells kill infected or abnormal cells.

scenes.tts: In mammals, inflammation gathers these defenses. Resident cells such as macrophages sense microbes with pattern-recognition receptors. Mediators such as histamine widen small vessels and loosen their lining. Fluid and plasma proteins, complement among them, leak into the tissue. Neutrophils squeeze out of the vessel, and monocytes follow. Macrophages then clear microbes and debris, and the tissue rebuilds.
scenes.visual: Tissue above a vessel bar: macrophage senses bacteria; mediators open a gap in the vessel wall; fluid and complement leak; neutrophils then monocytes squeeze out toward the bacteria; bacteria cleared.

scenes.tts: These numbers are illustrative, not a measured infection. Suppose one hundred bacteria enter a wound, and each doubles every twenty minutes. With no defense, four hours is twelve doublings: four hundred and nine thousand, six hundred bacteria. If defenses kill seventy-five percent each interval, the multiplier is zero point five, and the infection is cleared. If they kill only forty percent, the multiplier is one point two. About eight hundred and ninety-two bacteria remain, still growing.
scenes.caption: These numbers are illustrative, not a measured infection. Suppose 100 bacteria enter a wound, and each doubles every 20 minutes. With no defense, 4 hours is 12 doublings: 409,600 bacteria. If defenses kill 75% each interval, the multiplier is 0.5, and the infection is cleared. If they kill only 40%, the multiplier is 1.2. About 892 bacteria remain, still growing.
scenes.visual: Log-scale plot from the lesson's numbers: three lines from 100 over 12 doublings: no defense to 409,600, 75% killed to about 0.024, 40% killed to about 892.

scenes.tts: Assume constant rates and a well-mixed wound. Then the population shrinks only if two times one minus the fraction killed is below one. Keep one rule. In this model, a defense clears an infection only if it kills more than half the microbes in each doubling time.
